analysis.one_liner: Repeals the new medical device excise tax and pays for it by rescinding unspent stimulus money.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the medical device tax died in committee without a single vote; only the sponsor and 3 cosponsors ever signed on.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the 2.3% excise tax on medical devices that Congress created in 2010 to help pay for the new health care law. To cover the lost revenue, it would take back whatever stimulus money from the 2009 Recovery Act had not yet been spent. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medical device manufacturers, who would stop paying the excise tax on their products. The tax is paid by device makers and is largely passed through to hospitals, insurers, and ultimately patients and taxpayers in the form of higher prices, so the industry and parts of the health supply chain stood to gain most directly.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals section 1405 of the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, which imposed the excise tax on medical devices, and applies the tax code as if that section had never been enacted.
Offsets the lost revenue by rescinding the unobligated balance of discretionary appropriations from the 2009 Recovery Act (division A), meaning unspent stimulus money would be cancelled.

analysis.who_pays: Programs and jobs funded by unspent 2009 stimulus money, which would be taken back, and whoever would otherwise benefit from the revenue the device tax raised to finance health coverage under the new health care law.
analysis.who_pays_short: Unspent stimulus recipients and health coverage financing

drawbacks.text: The device tax was a dedicated funding stream for the health care law; repealing it without a replacement would open a hole in that financing, which is why the bill rescinds stimulus funds to offset the revenue.

Rescinding unobligated Recovery Act discretionary appropriations would cancel spending still intended for projects and programs during a weak economic recovery, a real cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

Device makers argued the tax burdened a relatively small, innovation-driven industry; defenders countered that a broad excise tax spread across a growing sector was a fair way to help pay for coverage that would expand the industry's customer base.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's direct benefit flows to one industry, while the cost is spread across health care financing and cancelled stimulus spending. Repealing the tax would modestly relieve price pressure on health care, but the offset—cancelling unspent recovery funds during a slow recovery—hurts the broader public, and the lost health-law revenue has to come from somewhere.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Appropriations committees on the day it was introduced, neither committee ever acted, and the Congress ended in January 2011 with the bill still sitting there.

narrative.text: Rep. Brian Bilbray introduced the bill on June 28, 2010, and it was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the House Appropriations Committee.
Three House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no further action of any kind appears in the record after the initial referrals.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill died in committee without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the medical device tax stayed in place as a funding source for the health care law, and unspent 2009 stimulus money was not rescinded. Medical device makers were denied a repeal they would eventually win years later under a different Congress; supporters of the health law's financing came out ahead for the time being.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The health law's financing and stimulus recipients

for.name: Rep. Brian Bilbray
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means and Appropriations referrals
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the medical device tax and rescind unspent 2009 stimulus appropriations.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; no hearing or markup appears in the record.

against.name: House Appropriations Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; the rescission of unspent stimulus appropriations fell within its jurisdiction.

sides.party_line_note: All four supporters in the record were Republicans (the sponsor plus 3 cosponsors), and no Democrat signed on; the bill was a Republican attempt to unwind a funding piece of the 2010 health care law.

industries.note: The bill would have removed the 2.3% excise tax on their products, a direct gain for the industry. That tax helped finance health coverage expansion that also grows the industry's customer base, so the industry's interest in this bill ran against the law's financing.
The bill's revenue offset would cancel whatever Recovery Act discretionary money had not yet been spent, taking funding away from planned projects and jobs during a weak recovery.

industries.industry: Hospitals, insurers, and health care payers
industries.note: Device taxes are commonly passed through into prices, so repeal would have modestly relieved cost pressure on hospitals and insurers. But the same payers benefited from the coverage expansion the tax financed.
